Trigger warning: What follows is a somewhat wonky explanation of election rules and procedures.
Advertisement
One choice, not two
Currently, a recall election is conducted in two parts. Voters are asked whether a lawmaker should be removed and, if so, who their replacement should be. If the incumbent is ousted, whoever gets the most votes takes their place, even if they fall well shy of attaining majority support. (Which is not out of the question in a large multi-candidate field; in 2003, 135 people were on the ballot (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-27-me-recallqa27-story.html), vying to replace Gov. Gray Davis (https://www.latimes.com/la-100703recall_lat-story.html).)
Among its provisions, Proposition 5 would amend the state Constitution so that voters would be asked a simple yes-or-no question: Do you wish to recall the incumbent? If so, the lieutenant governor would serve as governor for the rest of the ousted executive’s term — unless the recall occurred during the first two years a governor was in office and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election.
In that case, a special election would be held on the same date as the next primary and a candidate receiving a majority of votes would serve out the governor’s term. If no candidate received a majority, the top-two finishers would face each other in a November runoff, with the winner taking over as governor.
Still there?
Proposition 5 has two benefits. It would save taxpayer dollars by consolidating elections and it would enhance the legitimacy and political standing of a replacement governor by ensuring he or she assumed office with at least 50% support.
But there’s still more to be done (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2022-06-23/california-recall-reform-efforts-stall).
Ending political promiscuity
California makes it way too easy to qualify a gubernatorial recall measure.
Of the 19 states that allow their governor to be booted, California is by far the most permissive. Forcing an election requires signatures reflecting just 12% of the ballots cast in the prior gubernatorial contest. In Newsom’s case, proponents needed just under 1.5 million signatures in a state with more than 22 million voters and nearly 40 million residents.
Not exactly a thundering roar.
The threshold should be higher and the reasons for kicking a governor out of office should be more serious, such as corruption, official malfeasance or conviction for a serious crime. Not just because a governor is a member of the opposite party (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2024-03-01/newsom-recall-sore-losers-are-undermining-democracy), orpeople on the losing end (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-04-13/newsom-recall-revolt-red-vs-blue-california) of an election are unhappy with the result.
Advertisement
“The system in its current form offers bad actors an incentive to target an elected official with whom they disagree and to have the official replaced by someone who otherwise would not enjoy the support of a majority of voters,” Josh Newman of Fullerton and Isaac Bryan of Los Angeles said in advocating change. The two Democratic lawmakers authored the constitutional amendment, which was placed on November’s ballot by the Legislature.
If you think overhauling the process is simply about protecting partisan interests, consider: Should Republican Steve Hilton (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-22/gop-gubernatorial-candidate-steve-hilton-pleads-case-to-anti-trump-voters)pull off an epic upset (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-13/becerra-holds-strong-lead-over-hilton-in-race-for-california-governor-poll) and become California’s next governor (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-10/2026-california-election-governor-becerra-hilton-voter-guide), is there any doubt a recall effort would be underway before he and Mrs. Hilton even had the chance to start boxing their belongings for the move to Sacramento?
Voices
Barabak: Texas is red, California blue — but for how much longer? A Lone Star toss-up will tell (https://www.latimes.com/politics/newsletter/2026-09-03/midterm-election-california-texas-governor-senate-races)
A closely fought Senate race and competitive contest for governor have raised Democratic hopes, again. A Texas win would scramble the presidential map in 2028 and beyond.
Sept. 3, 2026
The recall is a vestige of the Progressive-era good-government movement. But the process needs to be revamped (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-09-15/california-costly-confusing-gavin-newsom-recall-rethink-the-rules)to reflect today’s bad-faith political environment.
The Little Hoover Commission, California’s independent oversight agency, has recommended several changes, including raising the signature requirement and prohibiting recalls undertaken during the first 90 days and the last six months of an officeholder’s term.
Elections, it’s said, have consequences. They also have — or should have — end dates and final results that are respected, not re-litigated until the losing side gets its way.
Proposition 5 is a step in the right direction. More should follow.

I now have a very comprehensive picture. Let me do one more check on the Sacramento Bee / McClatchy "yes" endorsement reasoning and any additional considerations (e.g., whether Prop 5 was criticized by legal scholars, whether there's a concern about the Lt. Gov being from a different party). Also let me check the Rose Institute or other nonpartisan analyses.

Actually, let me also weigh a critical detail: the AG's title/summary says "for all other recalled officers, the office will remain vacant until filled by a subsequent special election or appointment as specified in existing law." And "a recalled officer may be a candidate in a special election to fill the office."

Also note: Prop 5 changes Section 17 so that if the Governor is recalled, the SECRETARY OF STATE (not the Lt. Gov) performs the recall duties. That's a real good-government improvement: currently the Lt. Governor, who would directly benefit from the Governor's recall, runs the recall election. That's a blatant conflict of interest. Under Prop 5, the SoS handles it (and if the SoS is recalled, the Controller handles it). This is a meaningful improvement not mentioned much.

Let me verify that reading of Section 17. The text with strikeout/italic lost formatting:

"SEC. 17. If recall of the Governor or Secretary of State is initiated, the recall duties of that office shall be performed by the Lieutenant Governor Secretary of State or Controller, respectively. If recalls of the Governor and Secretary of State are initiated at the same time, the recall duties of both offices shall be performed by the Controller."

The Senate analysis says: "Provides that if a recall of the Governor is initiated, the recall duties of that office shall be performed by the SOS instead of the Lieutenant Governor. Provides that if recalls of the Governor and SOS are initiated at the same time, the recall duties of both offices shall be performed by the Controller."

Confirmed. So yes — Prop 5 removes the Lt. Governor's conflict of interest in administering a gubernatorial recall. That's a significant, under-discussed democratic improvement: currently the Lt. Governor (who has a direct personal stake in the Governor being recalled) is in charge of the recall election.

That's a strong point in favor.

Now let me weigh:

**Case for YES:**
1. Fixes the plurality-replacement problem: the single most undemocratic feature of CA's recall. A candidate can become Governor with far fewer votes than the incumbent received and less than a majority — even less than a third — of voters. In 2021, Elder would have become Governor with 27.8% of all recall voters while 61.9% voted to keep Newsom. In 2003, Schwarzenegger took office with 4.2M votes, fewer than Davis's 4.74M in 2002, and only 44.6% of all ballots cast.
2. Prop 5 requires a MAJORITY winner (with top-two runoff) in any gubernatorial special election — the standard applied to essentially every other California election.
3. Removes a glaring conflict of interest: currently the Lt. Governor — the person who directly benefits if the Governor is recalled — administers the recall election. Prop 5 shifts those duties to the Secretary of State (and the Controller if both are recalled).
4. Brings California in line with most of the 19 recall states: only California and Colorado put both questions on the same ballot; 5 states use snap elections, 7 use separate special elections, 5 use appointment/succession.
5. Consistency: it makes recalls work like every other vacancy (death, resignation), which voters already accept. In 2022, the Legislature already did exactly this for LOCAL recalls (AB 2582), which no one found controversial.
6. Cost: The 2021 recall cost $200.2M. LAO says net effect is unknown, could save or cost millions; less than 0.1% of the General Fund. Also, by raising the bar, it should deter frivolous recalls (182 attempts since 1913).

Under Prop 5, the SoS handles it (and if the SoS is recalled, the Controller handles it). This is a meaningful improvement not mentioned much.

Let me verify that reading of Section 17. The text with strikeout/italic lost formatting:

"SEC. 17. If recall of the Governor or Secretary of State is initiated, the recall duties of that office shall be performed by the Lieutenant Governor Secretary of State or Controller, respectively. If recalls of the Governor and Secretary of State are initiated at the same time, the recall duties of both offices shall be performed by the Controller."

The Senate analysis says: "Provides that if a recall of the Governor is initiated, the recall duties of that office shall be performed by the SOS instead of the Lieutenant Governor. Provides that if recalls of the Governor and SOS are initiated at the same time, the recall duties of both offices shall be performed by the Controller."

Confirmed. So yes — Prop 5 removes the Lt. Governor's conflict of interest in administering a gubernatorial recall. That's a significant, under-discussed democratic improvement: currently the Lt. Governor (who has a direct personal stake in the Governor being recalled) is in charge of the recall election.

That's a strong point in favor.

Now let me weigh:

**Case for YES:**
1. Fixes the plurality-replacement problem: the single most undemocratic feature of CA's recall. A candidate can become Governor with far fewer votes than the incumbent received and less than a majority — even less than a third — of voters. In 2021, Elder would have become Governor with 27.8% of all recall voters while 61.9% voted to keep Newsom. In 2003, Schwarzenegger took office with 4.2M votes, fewer than Davis's 4.74M in 2002, and only 44.6% of all ballots cast.
2. Prop 5 requires a MAJORITY winner (with top-two runoff) in any gubernatorial special election — the standard applied to essentially every other California election.
3. Removes a glaring conflict of interest: currently the Lt. Governor — the person who directly benefits if the Governor is recalled — administers the recall election. Prop 5 shifts those duties to the Secretary of State (and the Controller if both are recalled).
4. Brings California in line with most of the 19 recall states: only California and Colorado put both questions on the same ballot; 5 states use snap elections, 7 use separate special elections, 5 use appointment/succession.
5. Consistency: it makes recalls work like every other vacancy (death, resignation), which voters already accept. In 2022, the Legislature already did exactly this for LOCAL recalls (AB 2582), which no one found controversial.
6. Cost: The 2021 recall cost $200.2M. LAO says net effect is unknown, could save or cost millions; less than 0.1% of the General Fund. Also, by raising the bar, it should deter frivolous recalls (182 attempts since 1913).
7. Backed by nonpartisan good-government groups: League of Women Voters, California Common Cause, Secretary of State Weber, Dan Schnur (former Republican FPPC chair). McClatchy (Sac Bee) editorial yes; LA Times columnist Barabak and Skelton both yes.
8. It does NOT weaken the core recall power: the threshold to qualify, the signature requirements, and the majority-vote removal standard are all unchanged. Voters keep the full power to fire an official.

**Case for NO:**
1. Loses voters' immediate say on the replacement. For non-gubernatorial statewide offices, the GOVERNOR (with legislative confirmation) appoints the successor — an unelected politician replacing an elected one. That's a real transfer of power from voters to the executive.
2. If a Governor is recalled in the last two years of the term, the Lt. Governor serves out the term with no election at all — meaning a recall can't change the governing party or direction. In 2021, Kounalakis would have been Governor through Jan 2023. In 2003, Bustamante would have served at least until March 2004.
3. It raises the practical cost of a recall for voters: a legislative seat could sit vacant for months, and the deterrence effect could suppress legitimate recalls ("you'll be unrepresented").
4. The recalled official can run right back in the special election — a constitutional ban being repealed, which even the author can't explain. Undermines the point of the recall.
5. It's plainly partisan/self-interested: authored by a Democrat who was recalled; passed nearly on party lines; only Democrats + labor support it; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn, Reform California, CA GOP, Election Integrity Project oppose. The party in power is the party that benefits from making recalls less potent.
6. The independent bipartisan Little Hoover Commission — which studied this exhaustively — recommended a DIFFERENT fix: a "snap" election putting the incumbent on the ballot with challengers (which guarantees the winner gets more votes than the incumbent), plus raising the signature threshold to 10% of registered voters. Prop 5 does neither, and doesn't touch the signature threshold (among the lowest in the nation at 12% of votes cast).
7. Editorial opposition: SF Chronicle, Mercury News/East Bay Times, San Diego Union-Tribune, LA Daily News, OC Register. Only McClatchy papers + LA Times columnists support.
8. Polls: 35-59 in Sept, 45-52 in Oct — likely to fail.

Now, how do I weigh these?

Let me think about the strongest arguments on each side.

The No side's most substantive point: Prop 5 makes it possible for a successful recall to produce zero change in direction — the Lt. Governor (same party, same administration) takes over, potentially for the rest of the term. That does convert the recall from a tool of political change into purely a tool of personnel removal for cause. But is that bad? Arguably it makes the recall work as originally intended — "the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed" (Hiram Johnson). It prevents recalls from being used as a cheap "do-over election."

The Yes side's most substantive point: the plurality replacement is genuinely anti-majoritarian and creates a perverse incentive — a well-funded minority can force a recall hoping to install a candidate with 20-28% support. That's not a hypothetical: it's exactly what happened in 2003 and nearly happened in 2021. And Prop 5's remedy (majority winner with runoff in a gubernatorial special election) is a clear democratic improvement.

The counter to the "partisan" critique: the rule would apply symmetrically. If a Republican governor (e.g., Steve Hilton) were elected in 2026, Prop 5 would protect him from a recall-driven party flip too. Barabak makes exactly this point. And it's worth noting that the reform makes recalls harder to weaponize by whoever is out of power — which cuts both ways.

Hmm. But there's an asymmetry: Democrats hold nearly all statewide offices and a legislative supermajority. So in practice, Prop 5 protects Democrats far more often. That said, it also protects a Republican governor from being replaced by a plurality-winner Democrat, and protects Republican legislators from being replaced by a plurality-winner Democrat.

Now, the "recalled official can run again" flaw. How serious is it? It's odd, but:
- The Little Hoover Commission's own recommended "snap election" model puts the incumbent on the ballot.
- 5 other states (AZ, NV, ND, WI) automatically add the recalled official to the replacement ballot.
- Practically: someone just fired by a majority of voters is unlikely to win a subsequent majority-vote special election.
- And it only matters for offices filled by special election (legislators, and governors recalled in the first two years). For appointed offices they can't be appointed.
So the SF Chronicle's "glaring flaw" seems overstated — it's a real oddity but low-impact, and arguably more democratic (voters get to decide whether to bring them back, rather than a blanket ban).

The "governor appoints replacements for other statewide offices" flaw: this is the status quo for all other vacancies (death/resignation), and appointments require confirmation by a majority of each legislative house. And statewide executive officers other than Governor/Lt. Gov are not the locus of major policy direction in the same way. Also, the appointment lasts only until the next statewide election in most cases. Actually — for AG/SOS/Treasurer/Controller/Insurance Commissioner/SPI/BOE, the appointee serves until the next general election... Let me not over-claim. Under Art. V §5(d), the appointee holds office for the remainder of the unexpired term. Hmm, that could be up to ~4 years. That IS a meaningful loss of voter choice. But again — it's identical to the existing rule for a resignation or death. If Newsom's AG had died, the Governor would appoint a replacement for the rest of the term. So Prop 5 doesn't create a new power; it just applies the existing vacancy rule.

Actually wait — is that true? Under current law, if a statewide officer is recalled, the replacement is elected on the same ballot. If they die/resign, the Governor appoints. So Prop 5 makes recall = death/resignation for succession purposes. That's the LAO's framing: "changes the recall process to make it like the existing process for filling vacant state offices, except for the process to recall the Governor." Reasonable and consistent.

The strongest remaining objection is the deterrence/legitimacy argument: Prop 5 will make recalls less likely to succeed in changing policy, and will discourage voters from voting yes on a recall (fearing an unrepresented period or a same-party successor). That's a genuine reduction in the recall's accountability bite. And it's being done by the party that currently holds power, right after being targeted.

But: is the recall's "accountability bite" being reduced, or is its "election redo" function being reduced? The measure leaves intact the power to remove. And removal IS the accountability function. The "choose a new direction" function is what elections are for — and Prop 5 ensures that when a new direction is chosen, it's chosen by a majority in a real election.

Let me also weigh: how often does this matter? 11 recalls in 113 years, 6 successful. 182 attempts. This is a rare-event measure. The fiscal impact is under 0.1% of the General Fund. So the stakes are modest either way. The question is which default rule is better.

Considerations on balance:
- Prop 5 removes an obviously anti-democratic feature (plurality replacement, potentially with <30% support, fewer votes than the person being removed).
- It adds a majority requirement + runoff for the most important office.
- It fixes a genuine conflict of interest (Lt. Gov running a gubernatorial recall).
- It aligns California with the majority of recall states and with its own local-recall law (AB 2582).
- Its costs are speculative and small; the LAO says net effect unknown.
- Its drawbacks (Lt. Gov succession, gubernatorial appointment of other statewide officers, recalled official can run again) are either status quo vacancy rules or low-impact oddities.
- The No campaign's own answers to the Mercury News were remarkably weak and hyperbolic ("socialist oligarchy," "oppressed people eventually revolt"), and did not engage with the plurality problem at all — they just asserted the status quo is fine. That's telling.
- The No side's argument in the voter guide is largely ad hominem (attacking Newman for being recalled) rather than substantive.

The partisan-motivation concern is real but the measure's rules are facially neutral and would apply to a Republican governor identically. Good-government organizations that are nonpartisan (LWV, Common Cause) support it; a former Republican FPPC chair (Dan Schnur) signed the pro argument.

The Little Hoover Commission preferred a "snap election" model, but the Legislature chose a different approach, and the LHC's alternative (putting the incumbent on the ballot) has its own problems and would still allow a plurality winner. Actually, LHC's model guarantees the winner gets more votes than the incumbent — solving the core democratic problem too. But that model is used in only 5 states and the Legislature (SCA 3, Allen) didn't advance it. Prop 5's model is used in more states.

Hmm. This is genuinely close. Let me think about which way to lean.

Key question: does Prop 5 make California's democracy better or worse on net?

Better:
- No one becomes Governor with 28% support while 62% voted to keep the incumbent. That's a serious defect fixed.
- Gubernatorial succession requires a majority (with runoff) if there's an election.
- Conflict of interest in administering recalls removed.
- Removes an incentive to launch recalls purely as a backdoor path to office for candidates who can't win a normal election.

Worse:
- In the last half of a gubernatorial term, a recall can't produce a change of party/direction — the Lt. Gov finishes the term.
- Voters lose the immediate replacement choice for other statewide offices (gubernatorial appointment instead).
- Legislative seats may sit vacant for months; extra election cost.
- Recalled officials can run to win back their seat.

On the whole I think the pro side is stronger on the merits. The defect being fixed is concrete, documented, and occurred twice in 20 years; the harms are mostly status-quo vacancy rules and speculative costs. Also, the fact that most independent analyses (LAO) call it a fiscal wash, most recall states already work this way, and California already adopted this exact model for local recalls in 2022 (AB 2582) without controversy is telling.

One more consideration: does it weaken the recall so much as to be effectively a repeal? No — the removal power is untouched, and for legislators (the most common recall target — 9 of 11) there is still a special election where voters choose the replacement. So the "politicians choose your replacement" objection only applies to non-gubernatorial statewide offices, which have been recalled zero times in 113 years. In practice, Prop 5's effect is: (a) legislators → special election (voters still choose, just later, and with the recalled member allowed to run), and (b) governor → Lt. Gov succession, possibly with a majority-vote special election.

That's a much narrower and more defensible change than the No campaign portrays.

Let me also double check one thing: for a legislator recalled, does Prop 5 result in a special election within ~4 months? CalMatters says "the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember." Under Elections Code, the Governor must call a special election for a legislative vacancy; the LAO says "typically would be elected through a separate special election." So yes, voters choose.

Given all this, I lean YES.

But let me stress-test the NO case once more with the strongest version:

The strongest NO argument is the democratic-principle one: "If you vote to remove a governor, shouldn't you also decide who replaces them?" Under Prop 5, in the most consequential scenario (governor recalled in the second half of a term), voters who fire the governor get zero say over the replacement, and get a same-party successor for up to 2+ years. That is a real diminution of popular control over the most powerful office in the state. And the change is being made by the party that benefits, right after surviving a recall.

Counter: the Lt. Governor IS elected statewide by all voters, on the same ballot, in the same election as the governor. California voters separately choose a Lt. Governor every 4 years, knowing full well that person is first in the line of succession. That's not an "appointment by insiders" — it's a directly elected constitutional officer. And this is already the rule if a governor dies, resigns, or is impeached (e.g., if Newsom had been impeached, Kounalakis would have become Governor). So Prop 5 extends an existing, accepted, voter-legitimized succession rule to one additional circumstance.

Also, the No campaign's claim that "politicians, not voters, would choose" is simply inaccurate for the governorship (the Lt. Gov is elected by voters) and for legislators (special election). It's only accurate for the 7 other statewide executive offices, which have never been recalled.

That significantly weakens the NO case. And the Yes case's central claim (plurality replacement is undemocratic) is empirically solid and verified against official Statement of Vote data.

Additionally, the "recalled official can run again" flaw — SF Chronicle's deal-breaker — is actually consistent with 5 other states and with the Little Hoover Commission's own recommendation. And it arguably preserves voter choice: if voters fire someone for a reason that turns out to be unfounded, they can bring them back. The Chronicle's concern about unlimited recall-defense funds carrying over is speculative (and state law prohibits using recall funds for other campaigns, as the Chronicle itself notes).

Also worth noting: the No side raised/spent almost nothing ($40.5K by Reform California shared across multiple props), and the Yes side similar. This is a low-salience, low-money measure — voters are deciding on the merits. Polling shows No leading, but that largely reflects status-quo bias on a low-information measure and the fact that the ballot title ("Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers") is confusing — even the author admits the title may confuse voters since legislators aren't statewide officers.

I'm fairly comfortable: YES.

Let me do a final check on a couple of things: (1) the Sacramento Bee's yes rationale; (2) whether there are legal scholars opposing; (3) verify the Section 17 conflict-of-interest point is real under current law. Let me do one more round of searches to be thorough.

# SCA-1 Elections: recall of state officers. (2023-2024)
## LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
The California Constitution provides that voters may recall a state officer by majority vote and, in the same election, elect a successor with a plurality of the vote.
The Constitution prohibits an officer who is the subject of a recall election from being a candidate for successor.
The Constitution provides that the Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor when a vacancy occurs in the office of Governor, and requires the Lieutenant Governor to act as Governor during the impeachment, absence from the state, or other temporary disability of the Governor or of a Governor-elect who fails to take office.
When a recall of the Governor is initiated, the Constitution requires the Lieutenant Governor to perform the recall duties of the Governor.
...
If the Governor is removed from office in a recall election, this measure would provide that the Lieutenant Governor will become Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term.

Proposition 5 seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide.

# Bay Area News Group Editorial | Vote No on Proposition 4; reject Proposition 5
Proposition 5: Preserve Voting independence
When California Gov.
Gray Davis was the subject of a recall effort in 2003, he said in a televised speech at UCLA that he thought the recall would damage "the very fabric of our democracy."
Elected officials may not like to see accountability arrive earlier than expected, but that doesn't make Californians' recall powers a threat to democracy.
While Proposition 5 doesn't attack the people's ability to hold a recall election, it does tinker with how a replacement candidate is selected.
We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall.
Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.

That's another concrete example — Ling Ling Chang won SD29 with 31.8% while 42% voted against the recall. That's a strong, concrete, verified case. Actually the Sac Bee reported "Chang won with just under 34% of the vote" (of votes cast on the replacement question) — and 31.8% of the votes cast on the recall question. Either way, fewer than the 42% who voted no on the recall.

Let me confirm this. Newman recall 2018, SD-29: Recall question: 58.1% yes / 41.9% no. Replacement: Ling Ling Chang 33.8%, Josh Newman 25.4%(?)... Hmm, wait — Newman couldn't be a candidate. Let me check: candidates were Ling Ling Chang (R), Young Kim (R), Bruce Whitaker (D),... Chang got 33.8%. Total ballots ~65,000. So Chang got ~21,700 = 33% of ballots; "no on recall" got ~27,000 = 42%. So yes: Chang became senator with fewer votes than were cast to keep Newman.

This is exactly the Little Hoover Commission's concern: "current recall procedures breed the possibility of an undemocratic outcome since they allow a replacement candidate to win office while receiving fewer votes than the incumbent."

Let me verify quickly and then decide.

Actually I have enough. Let me do one quick verification search and then answer.

I'm now fairly confident in YES. Let me summarize the reasoning:

1. The core defect Prop 5 fixes is real, documented, and has produced anti-majoritarian outcomes twice in the last 25 years (2003: Schwarzenegger took office with 4.21M votes, fewer than Davis's 4.74M in 2002, and only ~45% of all ballots; 2018: Ling Ling Chang won a Senate seat with ~33% of ballots, fewer than the ~42% who voted to keep Newman; 2021: Elder would have become Governor with 27.8% of recall voters while 61.9% voted to keep Newsom).

2. Prop 5's replacement rule for the most important office requires a genuine majority (top-two runoff) — aligning recalls with the standard used in every other California election.

3. It removes a real conflict of interest: today the Lt. Governor — who directly inherits the governorship if the recall succeeds — is constitutionally in charge of calling and administering the gubernatorial recall. Prop 5 shifts that duty to the Secretary of State (Controller if both are recalled).

4. It leaves the actual recall power completely intact — signature thresholds, timelines, and the majority vote to remove are all unchanged. Voters keep full power to fire anyone. It only changes who picks the replacement and when.

5. It brings California in line with practice elsewhere: only CA and CO put both questions on one ballot among 19 recall states; 12 states use succession/appointment or a separate special election. And California already adopted exactly this model for local recalls in 2022 (AB 2582) without controversy.

6. Fiscal impact is a wash per the LAO (<0.1% of the General Fund); removing a 46-135 candidate replacement ballot saves millions while a consolidated special election costs millions.

7. The "No" side's central claim — "politicians, not voters, would choose your replacement" — is inaccurate for the two scenarios that have actually happened in 100+ years: legislators (9 of 11 recalls) get a special election where voters choose, and the governor is succeeded by the separately, statewide-elected Lt. Governor, or replaced by a majority-vote special election.

8. The flaws the opponents and SF Chronicle highlight (recalled official can run again; governor appoints successors for other constitutional offices) are modest: 5 other states and the Little Hoover Commission's own recommended model put the recalled official on the ballot, and gubernatorial appointment (with legislative confirmation) is already the existing rule for every death or resignation — Prop 5 just makes recalls consistent.

Against this: real partisan motivation, the Little Hoover Commission preferred a different fix, the deterrence effect could weaken recalls, and it's a low-salience constitutional change driven by the party that was recently targeted.

On balance, I think the democratic-defect fix outweighs. YES.

Let me do one last verification of the 2018 Chang numbers to be safe, and check the Rose Institute or another neutral source.

Actually, I'll just do one quick search to confirm the 2018 numbers.

California's Proposition 5 would remove the "replacement vote" after a governor is recalled; here's who would take charge
Prop 5, a constitutional amendment from former state Sen. Josh Newman, removes question two from state recall ballots. Governors would be succeeded by the lieutenant governor; other vacancies filled by appointment or special election. PPIC has it losing 35% to 59%.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 12, 2026
Link copied!

California recall elections are changing under Proposition 5, which asks voters in November 2026 to remove the replacement question from state recall ballots.
Proposition 5 would rewrite how California recalls state officials. Today a recall ballot asks two questions: whether to remove the officer and, if so, who should replace them, with the replacement chosen by plurality from a list that ran to 135 names in 2003 and 46 in 2021. Prop 5 removes the second question (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/). A recalled governor would be succeeded by the lieutenant governor; other recalled statewide officers would be replaced by the governor's appointment; recalled legislators would be replaced through a later special election. It is a legislative constitutional amendment, SCA 1 by former state Sen. Josh Newman, who was himself recalled in 2018, and it is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/). It also has the weakest polling on the ballot: 35% yes to 59% no in PPIC's September survey.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California’s November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure’s rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The case for the measure is majority rule. Under the current system a replacement can take office with far less than half the vote, and in 2018 Newman's replacement won the seat with 31.8% of the votes cast on the recall question, fewer than voted to keep him. The case against is voter choice: opponents say Prop 5 "takes away half" of the recall right by giving the replacement decision to "Sacramento political insiders." This explainer sets out what the amendment's text changes, the recall law it amends, what the state's 11 qualified recalls since 1913 show, what the Legislative Analyst's Office says it would cost, and where the campaigns, parties and polls stand with three weeks to go.

California's Proposition 5 would remove the "replacement vote" after a governor is recalled; here's who would take charge
Prop 5, a constitutional amendment from former state Sen. Josh Newman, removes question two from state recall ballots. Governors would be succeeded by the lieutenant governor; other vacancies filled by appointment or special election. PPIC has it losing 35% to 59%.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 12, 2026
Link copied!
Copy failed!
California recall elections are changing under Proposition 5, which asks voters in November 2026 to remove the replacement question from state recall ballots.
Proposition 5 would rewrite how California recalls state officials. Today a recall ballot asks two questions: whether to remove the officer and, if so, who should replace them, with the replacement chosen by plurality from a list that ran to 135 names in 2003 and 46 in 2021. Prop 5 removes the second question (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/). A recalled governor would be succeeded by the lieutenant governor; other recalled statewide officers would be replaced by the governor's appointment; recalled legislators would be replaced through a later special election. It is a legislative constitutional amendment, SCA 1 by former state Sen. Josh Newman, who was himself recalled in 2018, and it is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/). It also has the weakest polling on the ballot: 35% yes to 59% no in PPIC's September survey.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California’s November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure’s rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The case for the measure is majority rule. Under the current system a replacement can take office with far less than half the vote, and in 2018 Newman's replacement won the seat with 31.8% of the votes cast on the recall question, fewer than voted to keep him. The case against is voter choice: opponents say Prop 5 "takes away half" of the recall right by giving the replacement decision to "Sacramento political insiders." This explainer sets out what the amendment's text changes, the recall law it amends, what the state's 11 qualified recalls since 1913 show, what the Legislative Analyst's Office says it would cost, and where the campaigns, parties and polls stand with three weeks to go.

California's Proposition 5 would remove the "replacement vote" after a governor is recalled; here's who would take charge
Prop 5, a constitutional amendment from former state Sen. Josh Newman, removes question two from state recall ballots. Governors would be succeeded by the lieutenant governor; other vacancies filled by appointment or special election. PPIC has it losing 35% to 59%.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 12, 2026
Link copied!
Copy failed!
California recall elections are changing under Proposition 5, which asks voters in November 2026 to remove the replacement question from state recall ballots.
Proposition 5 would rewrite how California recalls state officials. Today a recall ballot asks two questions: whether to remove the officer and, if so, who should replace them, with the replacement chosen by plurality from a list that ran to 135 names in 2003 and 46 in 2021. Prop 5 removes the second question (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/). A recalled governor would be succeeded by the lieutenant governor; other recalled statewide officers would be replaced by the governor's appointment; recalled legislators would be replaced through a later special election. It is a legislative constitutional amendment, SCA 1 by former state Sen. Josh Newman, who was himself recalled in 2018, and it is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/). It also has the weakest polling on the ballot: 35% yes to 59% no in PPIC's September survey.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California’s November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure’s rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The case for the measure is majority rule. Under the current system a replacement can take office with far less than half the vote, and in 2018 Newman's replacement won the seat with 31.8% of the votes cast on the recall question, fewer than voted to keep him. The case against is voter choice: opponents say Prop 5 "takes away half" of the recall right by giving the replacement decision to "Sacramento political insiders." This explainer sets out what the amendment's text changes, the recall law it amends, what the state's 11 qualified recalls since 1913 show, what the Legislative Analyst's Office says it would cost, and where the campaigns, parties and polls stand with three weeks to go.

One more valuable data point: "in 2018 Newman's replacement won the seat with 31.8% of the votes cast on the recall question, fewer than voted to keep him." That's another concrete example — Ling Ling Chang won SD29 with 31.8% while 42% voted against the recall. So the plurality-winner defect has actually produced an undemocratic outcome in practice: Chang became State Senator with fewer votes than those cast to keep Newman.

That's a strong, concrete, verified case. Actually the Sac Bee reported "Chang won with just under 34% of the vote" (of votes cast on the replacement question) — and 31.8% of the votes cast on the recall question. Either way, fewer than the 42% who voted no on the recall.

Let me confirm this. Newman recall 2018, SD-29: Recall question: 58.1% yes / 41.9% no. Replacement: Ling Ling Chang 33.8%, Josh Newman 25.4%(?)... Hmm, wait — Newman couldn't be a candidate. Let me check: candidates were Ling Ling Chang (R), Young Kim (R), Bruce Whitaker (D),... Chang got 33.8%. Total ballots ~65,000. So Chang got ~21,700 = 33% of ballots; "no on recall" got ~27,000 = 42%. So yes: Chang became senator with fewer votes than were cast to keep Newman.

This is exactly the Little Hoover Commission's concern: "current recall procedures breed the possibility of an undemocratic outcome since they allow a replacement candidate to win office while receiving fewer votes than the incumbent."

Let me verify quickly and then decide.

Actually I have enough. Let me do one quick verification search and then answer.

I'm now fairly confident in YES. Let me summarize the reasoning:

1. The core defect Prop 5 fixes is real, documented, and has produced anti-majoritarian outcomes twice in the last 25 years (2003: Schwarzenegger took office with 4.21M votes, fewer than Davis's 4.74M in 2002, and only ~45% of all ballots; 2018: Ling Ling Chang won a Senate seat with ~33% of ballots, fewer than the ~42% who voted to keep Newman; 2021: Elder would have become Governor with 27.8% of recall voters while 61.9% voted to keep Newsom).

2. Prop 5's replacement rule for the most important office requires a genuine majority (top-two runoff) — aligning recalls with the standard used in every other California election.

3. It removes a real conflict of interest: today the Lt. Governor — who directly inherits the governorship if the recall succeeds — is constitutionally in charge of calling and administering the gubernatorial recall. Prop 5 shifts that duty to the Secretary of State (Controller if both are recalled).

4. It leaves the actual recall power completely intact — signature thresholds, timelines, and the majority vote to remove are all unchanged. Voters keep full power to fire anyone. It only changes who picks the replacement and when.

5. It brings California in line with practice elsewhere: only CA and CO put both questions on one ballot among 19 recall states; 12 states use succession/appointment or a separate special election. And California already adopted exactly this model for local recalls in 2022 (AB 2582) without controversy.

6. Fiscal impact is a wash per the LAO (<0.1% of the General Fund); removing a 46-135 candidate replacement ballot saves millions while a consolidated special election costs millions.

7. The "No" side's central claim — "politicians, not voters, would choose your replacement" — is inaccurate for the two scenarios that have actually happened in 100+ years: legislators (9 of 11 recalls) get a special election where voters choose, and the governor is succeeded by the separately, statewide-elected Lt. Governor, or replaced by a majority-vote special election.

8. The flaws the opponents and SF Chronicle highlight (recalled official can run again; governor appoints successors for other constitutional offices) are modest: 5 other states and the Little Hoover Commission's own recommended model put the recalled official on the ballot, and gubernatorial appointment (with legislative confirmation) is already the existing rule for every death or resignation — Prop 5 just makes recalls consistent.

Against this: real partisan motivation, the Little Hoover Commission preferred a different fix, the deterrence effect could weaken recalls, and it's a low-salience constitutional change driven by the party that was recently targeted.

On balance, I think the democratic-defect fix outweighs. YES.

Let me do one last verification of the 2018 Chang numbers to be safe, and check the Rose Institute or another neutral source.

Actually, I'll just do one quick search to confirm the 2018 numbers.

California's Proposition 5 would remove the "replacement vote" after a governor is recalled; here's who would take charge
Prop 5, a constitutional amendment from former state Sen. Josh Newman, removes question two from state recall ballots. Governors would be succeeded by the lieutenant governor; other vacancies filled by appointment or special election. PPIC has it losing 35% to 59%.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 12, 2026

California recall elections are changing under Proposition 5, which asks voters in November 2026 to remove the replacement question from state recall ballots.
Proposition 5 would rewrite how California recalls state officials. Today a recall ballot asks two questions: whether to remove the officer and, if so, who should replace them, with the replacement chosen by plurality from a list that ran to 135 names in 2003 and 46 in 2021. Prop 5 removes the second question (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/). A recalled governor would be succeeded by the lieutenant governor; other recalled statewide officers would be replaced by the governor's appointment; recalled legislators would be replaced through a later special election. It is a legislative constitutional amendment, SCA 1 by former state Sen. Josh Newman, who was himself recalled in 2018, and it is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/). It also has the weakest polling on the ballot: 35% yes to 59% no in PPIC's September survey.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California’s November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure’s rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The case for the measure is majority rule. Under the current system a replacement can take office with far less than half the vote, and in 2018 Newman's replacement won the seat with 31.8% of the votes cast on the recall question, fewer than voted to keep him. The case against is voter choice: opponents say Prop 5 "takes away half" of the recall right by giving the replacement decision to "Sacramento political insiders." This explainer sets out what the amendment's text changes, the recall law it amends, what the state's 11 qualified recalls since 1913 show, what the Legislative Analyst's Office says it would cost, and where the campaigns, parties and polls stand with three weeks to go.

PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Proposition 5 restores the recall to its original purpose: removing corrupt officials. It closes the loophole that allows replacements to win with a small fraction of the vote, reducing the politics and costs of future recalls. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause. Vote YES
CON
Proposition 5 degrades California’s century-old recall process by limiting voters’ right to select a replacement for recalled officials. Instead, when statewide elected officials are recalled, other politicians would choose a replacement. For lower offices, another costly, taxpayer-funded election would come months later, leaving the office vacant and the people unrepresented.

PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Election of State Officials. The State Constitution establishes legislative, executive, and judicial state offices. Some state officials represent parts of the state, known as districts. Other state officials, like the Governor or Attorney General, represent the entire state. Voters elect people to represent them in state offices for set terms. For example, a state Assembly Member is elected to a two-year term and the Governor is elected to a four-year term. To run for a state office, candidates must submit specific nomination documents before the election. State law sets when this “nomination period” occurs.
Recall of State Officials. The State Constitution allows voters to remove state officials from office before their term ends through a recall. A recall is an election in which voters are asked whether to remove an official from office. To qualify a recall for the ballot, supporters of the recall must collect a certain number of signatures from the official’s district (or statewide for statewide offices). Since 1913, 11 state recall efforts have qualified for the ballot (nine legislators and two Governors) and six have resulted in an official’s removal from office (five legislators and one Governor).
Two Questions in Recall Elections. In a recall election, voters are asked two questions: (1) whether the official should be removed from office and (2) who should replace the official if removed from office. The number of candidates appearing in the second question varies. For example, there were 135 candidates in the 2003 Governor recall election and 46 candidates in the 2021 Governor recall election. If a state official is recalled, the person who receives the most votes in the second question assumes the office.
Vacant State Offices. State officials may leave office before the end of their term for reasons other than a recall. For example, they may die or resign. When this happens, the office becomes vacant. The process to fill a vacant office varies by office. Typically, a vacant seat in the Assembly or Senate is filled through a special election called by the Governor. The Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor when there is a vacancy in the office of the Governor. Vacancies in other executive offices (for example, the Lieutenant Governor or Attorney General) and the Supreme Court and Courts of Appeal are filled by appointments by the Governor.
Frequency of Elections. Statewide elections in California are scheduled every two years. In scheduled election years, a primary election is held in either March or June, depending on the year, and a general election is held in November. In addition to scheduled elections, the state and local governments may call special elections to address specific issues. For example, the Governor may call a special election to fill a vacant Assembly seat.
Elections Administration in California. County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have election-related workload. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide .
Paying for State Recall Elections. State law requires the California Department of Finance to work with state and local elections officials to estimate the cost of a recall election for a state office. The department is required to send the estimate to the Legislature. The Legislature reviews the estimate and may provide funding for the election. Any remaining costs are paid by the Secretary of State’s and counties’ budgets.
PROPOSAL
As described below, Proposition 5 changes the recall process to make it like the existing process for filling vacant state offices, except for the process to recall the Governor.
Removes Second Question From Recall Elections. Proposition 5 removes the second question—who should replace a recalled official—from a recall election. This means, in future recall elections, voters would only decide whether to remove an elected official from a state office, not who would replace the official.
Specifies Steps for Filling Vacant Offices. If a state official is recalled, Proposition 5 makes the office of the recalled official vacant. Except for the office of the Governor, Proposition 5 uses the existing process for filling vacancies to fill the office. In the case of an office in the state Senate or Assembly, this means that a replacement typically would be elected through a separate special election. The Governor would choose who would fill a vacancy in any other office (other than office of the Governor).
Creates Separate Process for Filling the Office of the Governor. The process for filling the office of the Governor depends on when the recall occurs. If the Governor is recalled before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the term, Proposition 5 says that the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election. If the Governor is recalled later in the term, the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor for the rest of the term.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Fiscal Effects Depend on Frequency of Recalls and the Offices Recalled. Whether there would be costs or savings compared with today depends on the frequency of future recalls and the offices recalled. A recall of a statewide office (for example, Lieutenant Governor) would affect state elections officials and local elections officials in all 58 counties. A recall of a district-based office (for example, a state Senator or Assembly Member) would only affect state elections officials and local elections officials in those districts.
Potential Costs. Proposition 5 could result in higher costs associated with future recall elections if a special election is necessary to fill the vacant office after a recall. For example, a legislative office made vacant after a recall typically would be filled through a special election. If that special election could not be consolidated with a scheduled election, elections officials would need to run a standalone special election. The cost to state and local elections officials to administer such a special election could be millions of dollars per election.
Potential Savings. Proposition 5 could result in lower costs by removing the second question from the ballot. These savings would occur when a Governor is recalled in the latter part of the term and for other offices where vacancies are filled by appointment. There would be savings because ballots and voting materials would no longer include information about replacement candidates. The amount of savings would depend on how many candidates there would have been on the ballot if the second question remained but could be millions of dollars per election.
Net Effect Depends on Circumstances of Future Recall Efforts. The net fiscal effect is unknown because it depends on future recall elections. Proposition 5 could lead to savings or costs potentially in the range of millions of dollars to administer recall elections. How these savings or costs would be shared by state and county governments would depend on future decisions by the Legislature. This net fiscal effect represents less than one-tenth of 1 percent (0.1 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)

CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Under current law, voters decide at the same election whether (1) to recall a state officer, and (2) who will replace that officer if recalled.
Under this measure:
if the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor for the remainder of the term or until a successor is elected;
for all other recalled officers, the office will remain vacant until filled by a subsequent special election or appointment as specified in existing law; and
a recalled officer may be a candidate in a special election to fill the office.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
Net fiscal effect unknown. Possible state and local government savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer recall elections. These costs or savings would be rare, and depend on the office recalled and how often recalls occur.

PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 5
California’s recall process should protect our democracy by allowing for the removal of an elected official who is corrupt or abusing their power. It should never be used as a tactic to ‘redo’ an election as a political or partisan scheme. Proposition 5 will restore the recall to its original purpose by making it fair, democratic, and accountable to the will of the majority.
Under current law, a statewide recall ballot asks voters two questions in sequence:
(1) Should the official be recalled? (2) If so, who should replace them?
By being connected, these two questions create a dangerous loophole. An elected official can be removed by a narrow majority. Then, a candidate listed in question #2 can win the office with far less than 50% of the votes cast in the election. This encourages political actors to target officials they couldn’t defeat in a regular election and to install replacements who lack broad public support.
We saw this play out in the 2021 gubernatorial recall. Voters rejected it decisively. The recall lost by nearly the same number of votes that the Governor won the regular election with. But California taxpayers were forced to spend more than $200 million on an election whose outcome simply reconfirmed what voters had already decided. Nearly 70% of California likely voters called the effort a waste of taxpayer money. And had the recall succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with support from only about 28% of all recall voters.
Proposition 5 makes a single, commonsense change: it removes the second question from the recall ballot .
Under Prop. 5, in a state-level recall, voters would decide one very simple and important question: whether an officeholder should be removed. If a majority votes yes, that office becomes vacant and is filled under existing vacancy rules. If a Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would become Governor and if the recall occurs early enough, voters would elect a replacement at the next statewide election; other statewide officers would be filled by appointment under existing rules; legislative seats by special election. No shortcuts, no loopholes, and no replacement candidate winning office without majority voter support.
In most states with recalls, vacancies are already filled by succession or a separate election, not a same-day replacement contest.
By eliminating the second question, Proposition 5 removes the incentive and ability to weaponize recalls as a shortcut for partisan advantage. Recalls could not be gamed to overturn the results of regular elections or install candidates who couldn’t win under normal conditions.
The framers of our recall process intended to safeguard voters against corrupt and unaccountable officials, not to provide a weapon for political operators to undo election results they don’t like. Proposition 5 preserves the recall as a tool for accountability while preventing it from being used to sidestep regular elections and majority rule.
Vote YES on Proposition 5 to protect majority rule, defend taxpayers, and restore California’s recall process back to the voters it was designed to serve.
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
Darius L. Kemp , MPA, Executive Director
California Common Cause
Dan Schnur , Former Chair
California Fair Political Practices Commission
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 5
Disregard the mental gymnastics the other side is doing here to tie us in knots and try to make sense of the truly nonsensical.
They say Proposition 5 “protects democracy.” It does the opposite-it erodes one of the fundamental elements of our recall process: to choose who replaces the recalled politician.
That’s not protecting democracy-that’s protecting political elites.
They call California’s system a “dangerous loophole.” It’s worked for 100 years, ousting politicians who abuse their office and replacing them with whoever the voters decide will do better.
Proposition 5 would create a loophole, not close one. The other side is gaslighting you. They think you won’t notice. Don’t be fooled.
If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it. Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he raised taxes after breaking campaign promises.
Now, he wants to burn it down on his way out the door-making future recalls less effective and keeping politicians like him less accountable.
If you traded in your car, would you want to know what you were getting in return-or would you be happy to sign it away and let the salesman stick you in a jalopy of their choosing after you’ve already committed? That’s what Proposition 5 asks you to do.
Our recall system will continue to work just fine, if we don’t let political elites with sour grapes tinker with it to their benefit.
Vote NO!
Brian W. Jones , Senate Minority Leader
Joe Patterson , Assemblymember
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 5
Proposition 5 will take away your voice and erode your ability to remove and replace failed or corrupt politicians from office.
California politicians already have too much power. Proposition 5 gives them even more-and it does it by taking power away from you, the voters.
For over 100 years, California’s recall process has given us the ability to remove elected officials who abuse their office, break promises or fail to do the job they were elected to do. And, when that happens, the current process allows you-not politicians-to choose who replaces them.
Proposition 5 changes that system forever and takes power away from the people.
Today, a recall election asks two simple questions: Should the elected official be removed from office? If so, who should replace them? That means Californians can remove a failed politician and immediately choose someone new to take their place.
Proposition 5 keeps the first part but eliminates your ability to vote for a replacement.
Instead, Sacramento political insiders would decide what happens next. In many cases, politicians themselves-not voters-would choose who fills the vacancy, essentially allowing them to appoint another one of their friends or political allies to replace the one you just ousted.
In other cases, rather than an immediate replacement, the seat would sit vacant until another costly election-funded by you, the taxpayer-was scheduled months later. And here’s the kicker; that failed politician you just ran out the door for failure or corruption, they'd be allowed to run in that next election to regain control of the seat they just lost.
In either case, your vote matters less, and the political establishment gains more control.
Californians deserve the right to remove an elected official-and to choose who comes next. Proposition 5 takes away half of that right, and that’s wrong.
Supporters claim this measure improves democracy. It doesn’t. Democracy means voters-not Sacramento politicians-get to choose their leaders, when to give them the boot and who to replace them with. Proposition 5 undermines that fundamental concept.
Ask yourself: if you vote to remove a governor or another statewide elected official, shouldn’t you also decide who replaces them?
The answer is clear.
It’s also worth wondering why this measure is on the ballot in the first place. Why fix a system that isn’t broken and has been working just fine for over a century?
Well, the author of this proposal himself was recalled by California voters when he voted to raise gas taxes after promising not to. Instead of respecting the will of the people, he now wants to rewrite the rules and protect politicians like him from any meaningful accountability. California’s recall belongs to the people-not politicians. Protect your voice. Protect your vote. Protect your right to hold elected officials accountable.
Vote NO on Proposition 5.
Brian W. Jones , Senate Minority Leader
Joe Patterson , Assemblymember
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 5
Don’t be misled. Proposition 5 preserves your power to recall an official by majority vote while closing the loophole that allows a replacement candidate to take office with a small fraction of the vote.
Under current law, voters decide whether to remove an official by majority vote, but the replacement can win with far less than a majority. In 2021, a replacement candidate could have become Governor with support from 28% of recall voters. That is not majority rule.
Opponents want you to believe Proposition 5 takes away your right to choose. It does not. The real question is whether someone should become Governor with support from only a small fraction of California voters.
Proposition 5 preserves the recall while separating the decision to remove an officeholder from the decision about who should serve next. If a Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor-elected statewide by California voters-provides continuity of government until voters choose the next Governor through a regular election. Voters will still choose their elected officials. But candidates seeking statewide office should earn that office in a regular election based on their qualifications, record, and plans for California, not use a recall as a shortcut to power.
A recall should decide whether an officeholder remains in office. Choosing who governs should happen in a regular election, where candidates earn the support of California voters. Proposition 5 protects the recall, respects majority rule, and ensures candidates run on their own merits. Vote YES on Proposition 5.
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
Darius L. Kemp , MPA, Executive Director
California Common Cause

Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Recall Reform, Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment
Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023. As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters. The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024. The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process. Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled. If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law. Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor. If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The financial impact would depend on how often recalls occur and which offices are involved. Costs could increase by millions of dollars when a recall creates a vacancy that requires a separate special election, particularly for legislative offices. At the same time, eliminating replacement candidates from recall ballots could save millions in some elections by reducing ballot and election-material costs. Overall, Proposition 5 could result in either costs or savings of potentially millions of dollars per recall election, although the effect would be very small compared with the state’s overall budget.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s recall process so voters would decide only whether to remove an official, with the vacancy filled later under state law. A recalled official could run again, and the Lieutenant Governor would generally replace a recalled Governor.
NO: A “no” vote supports keeping the current recall process, in which voters decide whether to remove an official and simultaneously vote on who should replace that official if the recall succeeds.

Pro Con
Supporters argue that the current recall system can allow a replacement candidate to win with only a small share of the vote, particularly in low-turnout elections. They claim that Proposition 5 would make recalls more democratic and less confusing for voters while reducing opportunities to use recalls for political manipulation.
Opponents argue that voters should have the right to choose a Governor’s replacement at the time when they approve a recall. They say automatically allowing the Lieutenant Governor to take over could leave voters with a leader who shares the recalled Governor’s political views, limiting voter choice and weakening the purpose of the recall process.

Proposition 5
Delay replacing recalled state officials
Under current law, after choosing whether to recall an elected official, voters are asked who should replace them. This constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by state lawmakers, would delay the election of a successor until a separate election. The recalled officer would be allowed to run in that election. If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over their duties until a new governor is elected. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.

Summary
Support
Proposition 5 is a constitutional amendment born out of a proposal from the secretary of state’s office following the unsuccessful recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. Secretary of State Shirley Weber told lawmakers her office felt a recall election should focus on whether the elected official should be recalled, not whether other potential candidates would be better in the role. Democrat Josh Newman, who was successfully recalled from his state Senate seat in 2018, authored the measure, saying it would reduce the “political gamesmanship” that elevates candidates who otherwise wouldn’t receive a majority of votes.
Oppose
Opponents including the California Republican Party and Election Integrity Project, which advocates for voter ID requirements and restrictions on mail-in voting, argue that allowing the lieutenant governor to assume the governor’s position if the governor were recalled would dissuade people from participating in a recall election. Almost all legislative Republicans also opposed it, arguing that it would dilute the power of voters while protecting incumbents. The current recall process is how former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, was first elected in 2003.

Photo by NewsBase via AP Photo In summary Following the failed 2021 recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom, Democrats had the political will and momentum to call for changes to the recall process. What emerged was Proposition 5 on the November ballot, a measure to change the recall process. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat. She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.” A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms. If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins. “I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said. California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election. ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections. However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions. The ‘weak gazelle ’ Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman. In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 26 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes. Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election.
