Gov are often from the same party but can be from different parties (e.g., Davis (D) / Bustamante (D); Schwarzenegger (R) / Garamendi (D) / Maldonado (R); Brown (D) / Newsom (D)).

Also: If recalled in first two years, a special election with majority winner would be held — so voters do get to choose. Only in the last two years does the Lt. Gov serve out the term. That's consistent with how many states handle vacancies.

Let me look at how other states handle this to test the pro claim "In most states with recalls, vacancies are already filled by succession or a separate election, not a same-day replacement contest."

States with recall for state officials: Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Montana, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota, Oregon, Rhode Island, Washington, Wisconsin. Which use the "California style" simultaneous replacement question? California, Arizona, Colorado(?), Alaska... Actually:
- Alaska: recall → vacancy filled per succession law (Lt. Gov becomes Governor). Not simultaneous.
- Arizona: recall for state/local officials; for statewide, if recalled, the successor is appointed/elected per normal vacancy rules. Arizona does not have a replacement question on the recall ballot.
- Colorado: recall; the office is filled per normal vacancy procedures (for state legislators, appointment by vacancy committee). No replacement question.
- Georgia: recall of state officials → vacancy filled per law.
- Idaho, Kansas, Louisiana, Minnesota, Montana, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota, Oregon, Rhode Island, Washington, Wisconsin: mostly no replacement question.
- Michigan: recall of state legislators — vacancy filled by special election.
- Illinois: only gubernatorial recall (added 2011) — Lt. Gov becomes Governor.
- New Jersey: gubernatorial recall — Lt. Gov becomes Governor.
- Wisconsin: recall — special election held; but actually in Wisconsin, a recall election for state office has the candidate running against a challenger simultaneously, so the replacement IS chosen at the same time (head-to-head). That's different — a direct challenger.
- Nevada: recall — a replacement is elected at the same recall election (Nevada does have a successor question for some offices). Hmm, actually Nevada's recall: if recalled, candidates run for the office at the same election.
- California: unique in having a large plurality replacement field.

So the claim "in most states with recalls, vacancies are filled by succession or a separate election" seems broadly accurate. Let me verify quickly.

Also let me check what happened with Prop 5's polling trend: Sept 35-59, Oct 45-52. It's likely to fail but close-ish.

Let me now check LA Times endorsement, Sacramento Bee editorial, Mercury News editorial, and Ballotpedia.","format":"unknown","index":0}]

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.
Endorsement guide: S.F. Chronicle Endorsements for the 2026 California Election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Also: Y (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)es or no? Here are the Chronicle’s endorsements for California Supreme Court and appeals courts (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)
Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
But it is there. And the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure.
California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

## Process
### The Recall Election
Recalls vary based on how the successor is selected:
- Seven states hold recall elections simultaneously with election for a successor for most offices: Arizona, California, Colorado, Michigan, Nevada, North Dakota and Wisconsin.
- In five states, a recall election is followed by a separate special election for a successor for most state offices: Georgia, Illinois, Louisiana, Minnesota and Rhode Island (state legislature only).
- In eight states, a successor is appointed to fill a vacancy created by a recall election: Alaska, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island (offices of secretary of state, attorney general and state treasurer) and Washington.
In some instances, filling vacancies created by recalls differs by office.
Ten states—Alaska, Idaho, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Montana, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island and Washington— fill most state-level recall vacancies through special elections or appointment, but the office of governor is filled by the line of succession.
Rhode Island uses both the special election and appointment methods, depending on the office.

Proposition 5 : Change how recalled state officials are replaced
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 5 would remove the second question from state recall elections, the one asking who should replace the official if recalled. If a Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would become Governor, either for the rest of the term or until voters elect a new Governor, depending on timing. Other recalled offices would be filled the way vacancies are filled now: a special election for legislators and appointment by the Governor for most other offices.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 5 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 5
What changes State recall ballots would ask only whether to remove the official; no replacement candidates
Who fills a recalled Governor's seat The Lieutenant Governor, for the rest of the term or until a special election, depending on timing
Vote needed Simple majority
Legislature's vote Senate 32-8, Assembly 59-17 (August 2024)
Money No committee primarily formed for or against it. Against: $40,500 in outside spending by Reform California (shared with other props)
Latest public poll PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 45% yes, 52% no (likely voters)
Each figure is sourced in the sections below.
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , The details , How it got on the ballot , What would change , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 5 mean?
Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
What does a no vote on Proposition 5 mean?
Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
What would Proposition 5 cost?
The Legislative Analyst says the net effect is unknown. Separate special elections could cost millions of dollars each, while dropping replacement candidates from recall ballots could save millions. The Analyst says these costs or savings would be rare and depend on which office is recalled.
What it means for the City of LA
Proposition 5 covers only state officers: the Governor, other statewide officials, legislators and certain judges. Recalls of the Mayor, City Council members and other City officials follow the City Charter, which puts the recall question and the election of a successor on the same ballot; Proposition 5 does not change that. City residents would still vote in any state recall, and Los Angeles County's cost for the 2021 Governor recall was $52.9 million.
The details
Official title Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Legislative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by the Legislature (SCA 1, Resolution Chapter 204, Statutes of 2024)
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide. Under the State Constitution (Article XVIII, Section 4), an amendment takes effect if "approved by a majority of votes cast thereon."
The question on your ballot
Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: None submitted
This is not the Proposition 5 on the November 5, 2024 ballot, the measure on local bonds for affordable housing and infrastructure, which failed with 45.0% voting yes (Secretary of State, November 2024 Statement of Vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-general/sov/59-state-ballot-measures.pdf)).
What would change
Today If Proposition 5 passes
Recall ballot Two questions: remove the official, and who replaces them if removed (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)) One question: remove the official or not (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm))
Who takes office after a recall The replacement candidate with the most votes, even without a majority (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)) The office becomes vacant and is filled under existing vacancy rules (text, Art. II, Sec. 15(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Recalled Governor Replaced by the top replacement candidate The Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor. If the recall comes before the nomination period closes for the next statewide election in the first two years of the term, a special election is held with the next statewide primary, and a runoff at the general election if no one gets a majority. Otherwise the Lieutenant Governor serves out the term (text, Art. V, Sec. 10(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Recalled legislator Replaced by the top replacement candidate Seat filled by a special election called by the Governor (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm))
Other recalled state officers (e.g. Attorney General) Replaced by the top replacement candidate Governor appoints a replacement under existing vacancy rules (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm))
Can the recalled official run again? May not be a candidate to replace themselves (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf)) May run in the later special election, but may not be appointed to the seat (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/title-summary.htm); text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
The rules for qualifying a recall, such as signature counts and deadlines, do not change. A recall election must still be held 60 to 80 days after signatures are certified, or within 180 days if combined with a regular election (text, Art. II, Sec. 15 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
City recalls are not affected. Proposition 5 amends only Sections 15 and 17 of Article II and Section 10 of Article V of the State Constitution, which cover state officers (SCA 1 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1); LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)). Recalls of City officials follow the City Charter. When a City recall petition qualifies, the Council calls an election on whether to recall the officer “and if recalled, for the election of his or her successor” (City Clerk petition handbook, p. 21, citing Charter sec. 432 (https://clerk.lacity.gov/sites/g/files/wph1491/files/2021-03/lacityp_023253.pdf#page=21)). That two-part City process stays the same.
City voters and state recalls. City residents vote in any statewide recall and in recalls of legislators who represent them. In the 2021 Governor recall, Los Angeles County voters opposed removal 70.8% to 29.2% (Statement of Vote, recall question (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/16-question.pdf)).
Election costs. County election offices run state recalls. Los Angeles County reported $52,920,735 in costs for the 2021 recall, against a state allocation of $59,793,000 (Secretary of State cost report (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2021-recall/report-to-legislature.pdf)). The Analyst says Proposition 5 could raise or lower future recall costs and that the split between the state and counties “would depend on future decisions by the Legislature” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)).
We found no City Council or City Clerk position on Proposition 5 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
A constitutional amendment written by the Legislature needs a two-thirds vote of each house (SCA 1 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Jan. 30, 2023: Sen. Josh Newman introduced SCA 1. Assemblymember Isaac Bryan was the principal coauthor (SCA 1 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1); SCA 1 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Feb. 1, 2024: The Senate adopted it 31-7 (SCA 1 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Aug. 30-31, 2024: The Assembly adopted the amended version 59-17 and the Senate agreed 32-8 (SCA 1 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)). The Senate no votes were Alvarado-Gil, Dahle, Grove, Jones, Nguyen, Niello, Ochoa Bogh and Seyarto.
Sept. 10, 2024: Filed with the Secretary of State as Resolution Chapter 204 (SCA 1 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)). It appears on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot (SOS voter guide (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/)).
The 2018 recall of the measure’s author. Newman was recalled from the 29th Senate District in 2018, and Republican Ling Ling Chang was elected his successor on the same ballot (Secretary of State recall history (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/06-ca-recall-history.pdf)). The Daily News reports the recall passed 58% to 42% after Newman voted for a gas tax increase in 2017, and that he won the seat back in 2020 (Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/08/12/endorsement-vote-no-on-proposition-5-an-attack-on-californias-recall-power/)). The Sacramento Bee reports Chang won with just under 34% of the vote (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/proposition-5-could-change-california-s-recall-elections-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2cxbHa)).
Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. A constitutional amendment “if approved by a majority of votes cast thereon, takes effect” (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)).
Recall history. Since 1913, 11 state recalls have qualified for the ballot, nine against legislators and two against Governors, and six officials were removed (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm); Secretary of State recall history (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/06-ca-recall-history.pdf)). Two of the qualified recalls, both in 1994, targeted Los Angeles County legislators: Sen. David Roberti, who kept his seat, and Assemblyman Paul Horcher, who was removed (Secretary of State recall history (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/06-ca-recall-history.pdf)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the authors’ opinions and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm)). No supporters or opponents were listed on the ballot label (ballot label (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/)).
Argument in favor, signed by Lorrel Plimier of the League of Women Voters of California, Darius L. Kemp of California Common Cause and former FPPC chair Dan Schnur (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
The two linked questions are “a dangerous loophole”: an official can be removed by a narrow majority and replaced by someone with “far less than 50%.”
The 2021 recall “lost by nearly the same number of votes that the Governor won the regular election with” and cost “more than $200 million.”
Had the 2021 recall succeeded, the leading replacement would have taken office “with support from only about 28% of all recall voters.”
“In most states with recalls, vacancies are already filled by succession or a separate election.”
Argument against, signed by Senate Minority Leader Brian W. Jones and Assemblymember Joe Patterson (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
It takes away voters’ power to choose a replacement. In many cases, it says, politicians rather than voters would choose who fills the vacancy.
Seats could sit vacant until “another costly election.”
The recalled official could run in the next election.
The measure’s author was recalled by voters after he voted to raise gas taxes.
Outside the guide.
Carl DeMaio, who led the 2017-18 Newman recall, told the Sacramento Bee editorial board that politicians facing a recall could say “you won’t be represented for 12 months” (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/proposition-5-could-change-california-s-recall-elections-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2cxbHa)).
Newman told the Bee: “So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in’” (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/proposition-5-could-change-california-s-recall-elections-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2cxbHa)).
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association says the measure “makes a mockery of the recall process” (HJTA 2026 voting guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/)).
Checking the main factual claims against official records.
Claim Who makes it What the records show
The 2021 recall cost more than $200 million Yes campaign The Secretary of State reported a total cost of $200,241,680: $174,059,031.11 for counties and $26,182,649.08 for the state (cost report (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2021-recall/report-to-legislature.pdf)).
The 2021 recall lost by about the margin Newsom won by in 2018 Yes campaign Recall question: 38.1% yes, 61.9% no (Statement of Vote, 2021 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/16-question.pdf)). 2018 Governor: Newsom 61.9%, John Cox 38.1% (Statement of Vote, 2018 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-general/sov/07-summary.pdf)).
The leading replacement would have won with about 28% of recall voters Yes campaign Larry Elder led with 3,563,867 votes, 48.4% of replacement votes (Statement of Vote, replacement candidates (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/20-replacement-candidates.pdf)). That is 27.8% of the 12,838,565 votes cast on the recall question (our calculation).
Politicians would choose the replacement No campaign True for statewide offices other than Governor and Lieutenant Governor succession: the Governor appoints. Legislative seats go to a special election, and a recalled Governor is succeeded by the elected Lieutenant Governor (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)).
The recalled official could run again No campaign Yes, in the later special election; the official could not be appointed (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/title-summary.htm)).
Special elections cost more No campaign The Analyst says a standalone special election “could be millions of dollars,” and that dropping the second question could also save millions (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)).
We did not check the “nearly 70% of likely voters called the effort a waste” figure or the claim about recall rules in other states.
Who supports and opposes it
Supporters
League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause, which signed the argument in favor (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm); LWVC recommendations (https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/)).
California Democratic Party (CDP positions, Aug. 2, 2026 (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf)).
California Labor Federation and State Building and Construction Trades Council, the Sacramento Bee reported (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/how-would-prop-5-change-recall-elections-if-approved-by-california-voters/ar-AA2cvWMU)).
Former Sen. Josh Newman, the author (SCA 1 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Opponents
Senate Minority Leader Brian W. Jones and Assemblymember Joe Patterson, who signed the argument against (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (HJTA 2026 voting guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/)).
Reform California (Carl DeMaio), which reported spending against it (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
The legislators who voted no (SCA 1 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Editorial boards. The Los Angeles Daily News recommends a no vote (Daily News, Aug. 12, 2026 (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/08/12/endorsement-vote-no-on-proposition-5-an-attack-on-californias-recall-power/)). The San Diego Union-Tribune also says no (San Diego Union-Tribune, Sept. 25, 2026 (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/25/a-vote-against-prop-5-is-a-vote-against-the-california-status-quo/)). So do the Mercury News and East Bay Times: “Reject Proposition 5” (Mercury News, Oct. 20, 2026 (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/20/endorsement-no-on-prop-5-a-bad-idea-that-protects-the-status-quo-and-silences-independent-minded-challengers/)). So does the San Francisco Chronicle. It objects to the provision that lets recalled officials run in the special election to replace them and says “the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure” (SF Chronicle, Oct. 8, 2026 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-5-recall-california-22458510.php)). We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.
Editor’s note: To read our other recommendations for the most important races and measures on Bay Area voters’ ballots, please visit mercurynews.com/endorsements (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/13/bay-area-news-group-california-election-endorsements-november-2026/).

Money for and against
No committee primarily formed to support or oppose Proposition 5 reported raising money in 2026 in the Cal-Access data through Nov. 1, 2026 (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)). The Secretary of State’s contribution totals page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-5-sca-1-newman-elections-recall-state-officers-res-ch-204-2024) listed no committees, as of its Aug. 2 update, when checked on Sept. 30.
For Proposition 5 Against Proposition 5
Committees No 2026 committee. Newman’s “Californians for a Prosperous Golden State” ballot measure committee (ID 1466775) reported no contributions from Jan. 1 to June 30, 2026, then $28,402.34 from July 1 to Oct. 17, and had $11,112.49 in cash on Oct. 17 None registered
Other spending $25,352.15 in in-kind contributions from the California Democratic Party to Newman’s committee, Aug. 24 to Oct. 16. Independent spending through Oct. 25: $34,248.45 by eight committees, mostly shared with other props Independent spending through Oct. 25: $40,500 by Reform California (slate mailers, door hangers and campaign management, shared with other props) and $2,205.23 by the Republican Party of San Diego County
Source: Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip) (Nov. 2 export) and Newman committee statements (July 1-Sept. 19, amended (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3202517&amendid=1); Sept. 20-Oct. 17 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3216109&amendid=0); all statements (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1466775)), analyzed by CityHallPass. Of the $28,402.34, $25,352.15 was the Democratic Party’s in-kind help and $2,940.65 came from Newman’s committee for state superintendent.
Outside spending
Independent expenditures reported through Oct. 25, 2026 (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip) of Oct. 26):
Against: Reform California with Carl DeMaio (ID 1268914) reported $7,500 on July 1, $30,000 on Aug. 27 and $3,000 on Oct. 1. The same payments are listed against several other propositions, so the share spent on Proposition 5 cannot be separated. The Republican Party of San Diego County reported $2,205.23 for member literature on Oct. 5.
For: GrowSF ($14,511.76 for digital ads), SPUR ($5,822.64), Million Voter Project Action Fund ($5,299.08), Youth Power PAC ($3,815.67), two United Domestic Workers of America committees ($2,940.88 for mailers), Community Partners ($1,040.14) and AAPI Equity Alliance ($818.28). Most of these items are shared with other propositions.
Independent analysis
Legislative Analyst. The measure “changes the recall process to make it like the existing process for filling vacant state offices, except for the process to recall the Governor.” Net costs or savings could be millions of dollars per recall, less than 0.1% of the General Fund (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)).
Past replacement results. In the 2003 recall there were 135 replacement candidates, and 46 in 2021 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)). The Sacramento Bee reports Arnold Schwarzenegger won the 2003 replacement vote with 48.6% (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/how-would-prop-5-change-recall-elections-if-approved-by-california-voters/ar-AA2cvWMU)).
Recall attempts. The Sacramento Bee, citing the Secretary of State, reports 182 attempts to recall state officials since 1913, 11 of which qualified (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/how-would-prop-5-change-recall-elections-if-approved-by-california-voters/ar-AA2cvWMU)).
Interaction with other measures on this ballot
The Analyst’s analysis names no conflict between Proposition 5 and other measures on this ballot (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)). Proposition 39 (voter ID) also changes election rules, but for voting procedures, not recalls (Prop 39 title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/title-summary.htm)).
If it passes
When it takes effect. Five days after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)). It would apply to any later recall of a state officer.
Disputes. The State Supreme Court has exclusive jurisdiction over questions about a vacancy in the office of Governor (text, Art. V, Sec. 10(e) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
Legal challenges. We found no reported legal challenge as of Sept. 30, 2026.
Key moments
We found no debate focused on Proposition 5 in news coverage as of Sept. 30, 2026.
Newman recall (June 2018). Voters in the 29th Senate District recalled Newman and elected Ling Ling Chang (Secretary of State recall history (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/06-ca-recall-history.pdf)).
Governor recall (Sept. 14, 2021). Voters kept Gov. Gavin Newsom, 61.9% to 38.1% (Statement of Vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/16-question.pdf)).
Legislature passes SCA 1 (Aug. 31, 2024) (SCA 1 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Editorials split (August-September 2026). The Daily News and San Diego Union-Tribune said no; the McClatchy papers said yes (Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/08/12/endorsement-vote-no-on-proposition-5-an-attack-on-californias-recall-power/); San Diego Union-Tribune (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/25/a-vote-against-prop-5-is-a-vote-against-the-california-status-quo/); Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/proposition-5-could-change-california-s-recall-elections-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2cxbHa)).

# How To Fix California's Recall Elections
## Find out what's happening in San Diegofor free with the latest updates from Patch.
California’s recall ballot asks two separate questions of voters: whether the office-holder should be recalled, and if so, who should replace that person?
The problem is that while the officer-holder must obtain more than half of the vote on the first question to stay in office, a candidate on the second question needs only a plurality to win.
If the office-holder is recalled, whoever gets the most votes on the second question takes the office – no matter what share of the vote they receive.
This means that a replacement candidate can succeed to office while receiving far fewer votes than a recalled incumbent.

First, California should replace the existing two-part recall ballot with a “snap” special election, in which the targeted official appears on the ballot alongside the replacement candidates.
The voter faces a single, simple question: which of the candidates, including the incumbent, should complete the term?

This ensures no official is recalled and replaced by a successor with fewer votes. Prop 5 does NOT do that; instead it eliminates the successor election entirely and uses vacancy rules.

Also, the LHC recommended raising the signature threshold from 12% of votes cast to 10% of registered voters — Prop 5 doesn't do that either.

So the independent bipartisan watchdog recommended a different reform. The SF Chronicle noted Prop 5 "doesn't grapple with this issue" (signature threshold).

Also note: SCA 3 (Allen) 2020 would have eliminated the first question and automatically placed the official on the ballot as a candidate — that's the snap election model. The Legislature didn't adopt that.

Now let me also check:
- The Senate Third Reading analysis for SCA 1 (arguments pro and con in the Legislature).
- Whether there's any legal analysis pointing out issues (e.g., the recalled official could be re-elected; the Lt. Gov succession could produce a party flip issue).
- The Mercury News Nov 2 piece: "We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure."

Also: an important design consideration — under Prop 5, for non-gubernatorial statewide offices (AG, Treasurer, Controller, Insurance Commissioner, SOS, Superintendent), the GOVERNOR appoints a replacement with no legislative confirmation? Let me check: under current law, Art. V Sec. 5(d), the Governor nominates and the Legislature confirms (jointly) for certain offices. Actually California Constitution Article V, Section 5(d): "The Governor shall nominate and, upon confirmation by a majority of the membership of each house of the Legislature, appoint... [Secretary of State, Attorney General, Treasurer, Controller, Insurance Commissioner, Superintendent of Public Instruction, members of the Board of Equalization] ... to fill a vacancy in that office." So there IS legislative confirmation. The LAO said "The Governor would choose who would fill a vacancy in any other office."

Hmm — but note that this is the same as existing vacancy rules, so it's not a new power grab; it's the status quo for deaths/resignations.

Let me also consider: the biggest substantive objection is that it reduces the recall's potency as an accountability tool, in a way that systematically advantages the party in power (Democrats), because:
1. A recalled Governor is replaced by the Lt. Governor (usually same party) — so a recall can't change the governing party unless it happens early enough to trigger a special election.
2. For other statewide offices, the Governor (usually same party) appoints the replacement.
3. For legislators, a special election — neutral-ish, but with a delay and the recalled member can run again.

And supporters' counterpoints:
1. The plurality-winner problem is real and serious: Elder would have become governor with 27.8% of all votes, while 61.9% voted to keep Newsom. Under Prop 5, a gubernatorial special election requires a MAJORITY (top-two runoff). That's a genuine democratic improvement.
2. The Lt. Governor is separately elected statewide by all voters — so it's not an "appointment."
3. Most other states do it this way; California and Colorado are the only ones with the two-question format.
4. Fixes the conflict of interest where the SoS administers their own recall (Section 17 change).
5. Costs: 2021 recall cost $200M; removing the second question saves money.

The main flaw cited by neutral-ish observers (SF Chronicle) is the recalled-official-can-run-again provision, which even the author doesn't like. But note: 5 states (AZ, NV, ND, WI) automatically add the recalled official to the replacement ballot, and the Little Hoover Commission's recommended model does the same. So allowing the recalled official to run again is actually consistent with the LHC's recommendation and with practice in other states. It's only "bizarre" in the context where the official has just been fired by majority vote. Hmm — actually it's a real concern: voters fire someone, then that person can immediately run to get the job back. But the LHC's snap-election model does exactly that.

Now, importantly: the Mercury News argument that "if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante" — that's a legitimate historical point: the 2003 recall was a genuine change-of-direction mandate (1M more voters wanted Davis out), and under Prop 5 the outcome would have been different — Bustamante (D) would have become governor, and the recall would have effectively been a no-op in terms of party/policy direction. Actually wait — Davis was recalled in October 2003, which was in year 1 of his second term (elected Nov 2002). Under Prop 5's rules, if recalled before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the term, a special election would be held consolidated with the next statewide primary — March 2004 — and a runoff in Nov 2004. So voters WOULD have chosen a new governor, with a majority requirement. Schwarzenegger might well have won that too (he was the front-runner). So the Mercury News's claim that Bustamante would have succeeded Davis isn't quite right given the timing rule — actually the Mercury News said "Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante" [in the interim] "who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election." Hmm, arguable. But at least there'd be an election with a majority requirement, and Schwarzenegger could have run (and he was quite popular). So the Mercury News's argument is somewhat overstated.

Whereas in 2021 (Sept 2021), Newsom was recalled... he was in year 3 of his first term (elected Nov 2018, term started Jan 2019). Actually the recall was in the second half of the first term → under Prop 5, the Lt. Governor (Eleni Kounalakis, D) would have become Governor for the remainder of the term (until Jan 2023), with NO election. Hmm wait: "before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the Governor's term" — Newsom's first two years were Jan 2019 – Jan 2021. The recall was Sept 2021, i.e., after the first two years. So Kounalakis would have served until Jan 2023. That's a case where a recall that a majority approved (hypothetically) would hand power to the same party without any election. That is the strongest argument against Prop 5.

So the trade-off is real:
- Prop 5 protects against undemocratic plurality replacements, but in exchange it can hand power to a same-party successor with no election at all.

Also, let me check whether there's any notable "Yes" support from Republicans or independents — Dan Schnur (former FPPC chair, formerly Republican, now USC professor) signed the argument in favor. And the "Californians for a Prosperous Golden State" committee. GrowSF and SPUR (YIMBY groups) spent in support.

SUBJECT: Elections: recall of state officers
SOURCE: Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber, Ph.D
California Common Cause
League of Women Voters of California
DIGEST: This constitutional amendment, if approved by voters, eliminates the
successor election for a recalled state officer and provides, in the event an officer is
removed in a recall election, that the office will remain vacant until it is filled in
accordance with existing law. This constitutional amendment also repeals the
prohibition against the officer subject to the recall from being a candidate to fill the
office in a special election, but prohibits the appointment of the officer subject to
the recall election to fill the vacancy.
ANALYSIS:
Existing law:
1) States, pursuant to the California Constitution, that the recall is the power of
the voters to remove an elective officer.
SCA 1
Page 2
2) Provides that a recall of a state officer is initiated by delivering to the Secretary
of State (SOS) a petition alleging reason for recall. Provides that sufficiency
of reason is not reviewable.
3) Provides that proponents have 160 days to file signed petitions. Provides that a
petition to recall a statewide officer must be signed by electors equal in number
to 12 percent of the last vote for the office, with signatures from each of five
counties equal in number to one percent of the last vote for the office in the
county. Requires that signatures to recall Senators, members of the Assembly,
members of the Board of Equalization, and judges of courts of appeal and trial
courts equal 20 percent of the last vote for the office. Requires the SOS
maintain a continuous count of the signatures certified to that office.
4) Provides that an election to determine whether to recall an officer and, if
appropriate, to elect a successor shall be called by the Governor and held not
less than 60 days nor more than 80 days from the date of certification of
sufficient signatures. Provides that a recall election may be conducted within
180 days from the date of certification of sufficient signatures in order that the
election may be consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election
occurring wholly or partially within the same jurisdiction in which the recall
election is held, if the number of voters eligible to vote at that next regularly
scheduled election equals at least 50 percent of all the voters eligible to vote at
the recall election.
5) Provides that if the majority vote on the question is to recall, then the officer is
removed. Provides that if there is a candidate who receives a plurality, they are
the successor. Prohibits the targeted state officer from being a successor
candidate. Prohibits a successor candidacy for a judicial vacancy if the judge
is recalled, as specified.
6) Requires the Legislature to provide for circulation, filing, certification of
petitions, nomination of candidates, and the recall election.
7) Provides that if a recall of the Governor or SOS is initiated, the recall duties of
that office shall be performed by the Lieutenant Governor or Controller,
respectively.
8) Provides that a state officer who is not recalled shall be reimbursed by the
State for the officer’s recall election expenses legally and personally incurred.
SCA 1
Page 3
Prohibits another recall from being initiated against the officer until six months
after the election.
9) Requires the Legislature to provide for the recall of local officers unless a
county or city provides for recall within their respective charters.
10) Requires a local recall election to include only the question of whether the
local elected officer should be removed from office, as specified. Prohibits the
successor election for a local office from occurring at the same time as the
recall election of a local elected officer, and requires the office, if a local
officer is recalled, to become vacant until the position is filled according to
existing law.
This constitutional amendment:
1) Eliminates the successor election for a recalled state officer and would provide,
in the event an officer is removed in a recall election, that the office will
remain vacant until it is filled in accordance with existing law. Repeals the
prohibition against the officer subject to the recall from being a candidate to
fill the office in a special election, but prohibits the appointment of the officer
subject to the recall election to fill the vacancy.
2) Provides that if a recall of the Governor is initiated, the recall duties of that
office shall be performed by the SOS instead of the Lieutenant Governor.
Provides that if recalls of the Governor and SOS are initiated at the same time,
the recall duties of both offices shall be performed by the Controller.
3) Requires, notwithstanding a specified section in the California Constitution,
the Lieutenant Governor become Governor for the remainder of the unexpired
term that if the Governor is removed from office by recall. Provides that if the
Governor is removed from office by recall before the close of the nomination
period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the
Governor’s term, a special election shall be called to replace the Governor, be
consolidated with the statewide primary election, and, if necessary, the
subsequent statewide general election. Provides that if a candidate receives a
majority of the votes in the special election that is consolidated with the
statewide primary election, that candidate shall become Governor for the
remainder of the unexpired term. Provides that if no candidate receives a
majority of the votes, the top two vote-getters shall compete in a special
election consolidated with the subsequent statewide general election, and the
SCA 1
Page 4
winner of that election shall become Governor for the remainder of the
unexpired term.
4) Makes corresponding formatting changes.
Background
Informational Recall Hearings. During the 2021-22 legislative session, the
Assembly Committee on Elections and the Senate Elections and Constitutional
Amendments Committee held a series of joint informational hearings to review
California’s recall process following the previous gubernatorial recall election.
At the first hearing on October 28, 2021, the committees heard from current and
former elected officials, elections experts, and academics about their perspectives
on the state’s recall process and different reform proposals, including increasing
the number of signatures for qualifying a statewide recall and changing the method
for selecting the successor to a recalled official.
At the second hearing on December 6, 2021, the committees heard from two panels
of expert witnesses. The first panel of academics examined a limitation used in
several states which only allows recalls to be initiated against an official for certain
enumerated causes. The second panel of experts and local elected officials
discussed the use of the recall at the local level, along with potential options for
reform.
At the third and final recall informational hearing on February 1, 2022, the
committees heard from the SOS who shared recommendations for improvements
on the state recall process based on her consultation with outside experts and
stakeholders. The committees also received an overview from Dr. Mark
Baldassare, President and Chief Executive Officer of the Public Policy Institute of
California (PPIC), regarding its January 2022 statewide survey in which the PPIC
asked Californians about their views on the recall process. Dr. Baldassare
presented new data from their statewide survey and discussed whether and how the
views of California voters about the recall process have changed since statewide
surveys that PPIC conducted in July and November of last year.
One of the major takeaways from the committee’s first two hearings was that many
of the recall reform proposals would require voter approval in order to take effect.
In particular, proposals to make significant structural changes to the recall process
at the state level generally require an amendment to the California Constitution.
By contrast, changes to the process for recalling local elected officials and certain
SCA 1
Page 5
procedural changes to the state process can be made through statutory changes
alone. The third hearing generally reinforced the importance of continuing to
evaluate California’s recall processes and that California voters generally support
reform of the recall process, but are against any changes to the recall procedure or
process that diminish or decrease the voter’s power to recall an elected official.
Recent Changes to Local Recall Elections. In 2022, the Legislature passed and
Governor Newsom signed AB 2582 (Bennett, Chapter 790, Statutes of 2022).
AB 2582 made changes to the two-question process for the recall of local officers
in jurisdictions that do not have a charter providing for recall. Specifically,
AB 2582 removed the successor candidate question from the recall question, so
that the election for a local officer only includes the question of whether the officer
sought to be recalled shall be removed from office.
History of Recall Elections. According to the SOS, since 1913 there have been
179 recall attempts of state elected officials in California (trial court judges are
considered local officials for the purposes of state statutes governing recalls and
are not included in these figures). Eleven recall efforts collected enough signatures
to qualify for the ballot. Of the 11 recall elections, the elected official was recalled
in six instances. Below is a list of recall attempts of state officials that have
qualified for the ballot and the outcome of the election:
Year Officer Outcome
1913 Senator Marshall Black Recalled
1913 Senator Edwin E. Grant Recalled
1914 Senator James C. Owens Unsuccessful
1994 Senator David Roberti Unsuccessful
1994 Assemblymember Michael Machado Unsuccessful
1994 Assemblymember Paul Horcher Recalled
1995 Assemblymember Doris Allen Recalled
2003 Governor Gray Davis Recalled
2007 Senator Jeffrey Denham Unsuccessful
2018 Senator Josh Newman Recalled
2021 Governor Gavin Newsom Unsuccessful
Little Hoover Commission. The Little Hoover Commission (LHC) launched a
study in 2021 to consider whether the state’s system for recalling state office-
holders should be changed, and if so, how. The study resulted in its 2022 report,
“Reforming the Recall.” In the report, the LHC concluded that the recall system
should be retained, both because it is substantively valuable – voters should be able
SCA 1
Page 6
to fire an elected official mid-term – and because it is overwhelmingly popular
with voters. However, the report also concluded that substantial changes are
needed in California’s recall process.
According to the report, current recall procedures breed the possibility of an
undemocratic outcome since they allow a replacement candidate to win office
while receiving fewer votes than the incumbent. There is also concern that the
recall is subject to potential overuse or abuse. The report made various
recommendations, including replacing the existing two-part recall ballot with a
“snap” special election in which the official targeted for recall is placed on the
ballot with all replacement candidates.
Comments
According to the author, California’s recall provisions were conceived of and
enacted more than 110 years ago. Obviously, the world has changed quite a bit
since then, and sadly, politics is no exception. The system in its current form
offers bad actors an incentive to target an elected official with whom they disagree
and to have the official replaced by someone who otherwise would not enjoy the
support of a majority of voters. SCA 1 will ensure that statewide and legislative
recalls in California are democratic, fair, and not subject to political
gamesmanship. This constitutional amendment will adjust how state-level recall
elections are conducted, so that only one question will appear on a recall ballot,
asking a voter to decide whether or not an elected official should be recalled from
office. If a recall is successful, the official will be replaced in the manner
consistent with existing law if the official were to leave office for any other reason.
Related/Prior Legislation
AB 2582 (Bennett, Chapter 790, Statutes of 2022) changed the two-question
process for the recall of local officers in jurisdictions that do not have a charter
providing for recall by removing the successor candidate question from the recall
question, so that the election for a local officer to only include the question of
whether the officer sought to be recalled shall be removed from office and, if
successful, if filled by existing laws for vacated offices.
AB 2584 (Berman, Chapter 791, Statutes of 2022) increased the total number of
proponents required to be included on a notice of intention to recall an elected
officer, established a public display period for local recall petitions, authorized a
voter to seek a writ of mandate or injunction requiring any or all of the statement
of the proponents or answer of the officer to be amended or deleted on a recall
SCA 1
Page 7
petition, required a petition for the recall of a school board member to contain a
fiscal estimate of the cost for conducting the recall election, and changed the
timeframe for when a qualified local recall election is held.

eliminated the second question on the recall ballot that asks which candidate
should replace the recalled official, and instead generally requires the office, if the
state officer is recalled, to become vacant and to be filled in accordance with
existing law. SCA 6 was referred to the Senate Elections and Constitutional
Amendment Committee, but was not heard.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does Prop. 5 solve?
In its current form, a state-level recall ballot asks two questions in sequence: first, whether to remove an elected official, and second, who should immediately replace them. Although removal requires a majority vote, replacement doesn’t; whoever gets the most votes takes office, even if it’s by a small plurality in a crowded field. That mismatch can mean that an officeholder ousted by majority vote can be replaced by someone with far less support, and it gives well-organized interest groups a powerful incentive to instigate a recall in order to install a preferred candidate who wouldn’t have majority support under normal conditions. Prop. 5 fixes that mismatch by removing the replacement question and filling a vacancy under existing succession law instead.

We asked the No on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
Why is this the best solution?
Prop. 5 is the best solution because it fixes the specific, politically exploitable flaw — the plurality replacement provision — while still maintaining the recall as a powerful tool of direct democracy. Under its provisions, if a governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor, already duly elected by a majority of Californians statewide, steps in. If a recall takes place in the first two years of the term and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election, voters would still get a special election for a permanent successor, with a runoff if needed to achieve a majority. If the recall takes place later in the term, the lieutenant governor would serve out the remainder of an ousted governor’s term, the same as if they were to leave office for some other reason. In the event of a recall of other state-level officers, those offices would be filled under existing vacancy replacement provisions.
Why would Californians want to remove someone from office but forfeit to the governor their current right to immediately choose a successor?
Two corrections worth making: In the event of a gubernatorial recall, it wouldn’t be the governor who gains power but the lieutenant governor, a separately elected constitutional officer who is, by virtue of California’s Constitution, explicitly and deliberately next in the line of succession. Intrinsic to any lieutenant governor’s campaign is the assertion that he or she is most qualified to step in if events so demand. Second, voters aren’t forfeiting a choice: If a governor is recalled early in their term, Californians would still elect a permanent successor by majority through a special election. This is a sensible change from the current format, where, in the event of a gubernatorial recall, a replacement candidate can become governor of the largest and most important state in the country with only a small plurality, in a special election decided by a reduced electorate in a low-information and highly politicized environment.
Explain how this empowers majority rule and why that matters.
As it currently stands, while recalling a state-level elected official requires majority support, replacing them doesn’t. Only a plurality is required, which could be as low as 20% in a crowded replacement field. Prop. 5 closes that gap. When a successor election is held, if no one wins a majority outright, it would go to a runoff. So, whoever ultimately holds the office would have secured the support of more than half the voters, not just the largest slice of a fractured field. This is the standard California already applies to nearly every other office and election scenario. A recall shouldn’t be the one process where a candidate can take power without the validation of majority voter support.
How does this measure stop political groups from abusing the recall process?
It removes the existing incentive for political gamesmanship at the expense of electoral integrity. As it stands, a well-funded, motivated minority can force a recall and realistically expect its preferred candidate to win the replacement seat with a small plurality, sometimes far fewer votes than the officeholder who was removed. That’s a low bar for a high-value prize, and it’s why some recalls have been criticized as backdoor attempts to grab a seat that couldn’t be won in a regular election. Prop. 5 raises the bar and removes that incentive: Voters will still be able to remove a corrupt or malfeasant official, but it removes the strategic upside of gaming a plurality-only replacement. Instead, a replacement would be made in the normal order, and in the next election, the winner would ultimately secure a majority, with a runoff if needed.
How would this save taxpayers money?
First and foremost, by changing the incentive structure by eliminating the second question, Prop. 5 would save taxpayers money by reducing the likelihood of hyperpartisan recalls like the one which targeted Gov. Newson in 2021, which cost California taxpayers more than $200 million dollars in the midst of an unprecedented public health emergency where those funds were desperately needed for other purposes. Newly elected then-California Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger with wife, Maria Shriver, waves to supporters from the stage following his victory in the California recall election at the Century Plaza Hotel in 2003 in Los Angeles, California.
By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 4:32 PM PST | UPDATED: November 3, 2026 at 4:35 AM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What problem would Prop. 5 create?
A disincentive for the people to self-govern, leading to more distrust of government and restlessness of the “masses.” After a time of withdrawal and lack of participation, the people will feel and react to their oppression in a negative way. Oppressed people eventually revolt, and it’s never pretty.
Related Articles
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
Currently, the recall process allows a candidate to win office without a majority. Why is that a system not worth reforming?
Under the current system, the democratic process of self-governance is served, and infinite amounts of taxpayer funds are saved by the current one-step process.
Prop. 5 “reforms” the current process by taking power from the people, and — worse — punishing the people for having the audacity to self-govern.
In the case of a recall, the term of office is limited to the remainder of the term of the recalled individual, and awarding the win to the person receiving a plurality in a crowded field is much more protective of the “democratic process” than adopting the changes proposed by Prop. 5, where the Sacramento insiders are the winners, hundreds of millions of dollars are wasted, and democracy dies.
If this measure isn’t a solution for fixing the recall process, do you have an alternate proposal?
This question pre-supposes the recall process needs fixing. The current process, wherein a recall decision and a filling of the recalled position in the case of recall success on the same ballot is efficient, fiscally responsible and respectful to the public.
The suggestion that the cost of having part two of the recall ballot is negligible, let alone millions of dollars, is patently absurd. Also absurd is the Prop. 5 proposal to eventually fill the recalled position with another, delayed election. The cost of a second election, which is likely to lead to a runoff costing more millions, is unarguable. That’s the very definition of absurd.
To quote Sen. Jones, “Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he (voted to raise) taxes after breaking campaign promises.”
What’s the biggest misconception about Prop. 5?
That there’s something wrong with the current system, and that CA legislators have any respect for a government of, by and for the people. CA is no longer a republic, but a socialist oligarchy. The power of the people to govern themselves has been so diminished already as to be virtually eliminated, and Prop. 5 is another step to seal the deal for complete power of the elite.
What did we miss? What didn’t we ask that our readers should know?
The element of Prop. 5 dealing with gubernatorial succession is also faulty. Yes, the people ostensibly elected a lieutenant governor, to serve as governor in the event of incapacity or death of the elected governor, not in the event of the governor’s disgrace — by which the lieutenant governor is surely tainted.
If the lieutenant governor wishes to succeed the governor in the event of a recall, that person may appear on the second portion of the ballot.
Chances are virtually 100% that if the people have grown disenchanted with the governor’s performance, they will be equally unwilling to be represented in that office by the second in command — almost certainly complicit in every act of disappointment and betrayal by the governor.

That was the tab in 2021, when California held a recall election (https://www.latimes.com/topic/newsom-recall) less than a year before Gov. Gavin Newsom was set to face voters.
There was angst —the COVID-19 pandemic was raging (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-19/l-a-county-covid-19-deaths-top-25000-as-delta-spreads). There was anger — the lifesaving restrictions (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-12-13/california-orders-statewide-mask-order-starting-wednesday) imposed by Washington and Sacramento made daily living a chore (https://www.latimes.com/science/coronavirus-one-year-later) and drove many small businesses to the brink. Others went clear over the edge (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2020-10-29/coronavirus-pandemic-small-business-southern-california).
There was also no small amount of political opportunism at play.
The recall gave Newsom’s critics, mainly on the right, a chance to try to chase the Democrat from an office (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-27/recall-backers-have-california-ideas-beyond-newsom-defeat) that Republicans, under normal circumstances, stood little chance of winning.
Advertisement
In the end, the recall effort amounted to scarcely more than a partisan tantrum. The result — 61.9% voting no, 38.1% voting yes (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-09-14/recall-election-california-newsom-results) — matched the outcome of the 2018 gubernatorial race (https://www.latimes.com/politics/la-pol-ca-california-governor-race-20181106-story.html) down to the decimal. All that money and effort wasted on an election in which voters said pretty much, yep, we meant what we said. Not too long after, they gave Newsom a second term (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-11-08/2022-california-election-governor-newsom-dahle-results).
The plebiscite, and its pointlessness (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-09-15/newsom-california-recall-election-costly-lessons), underscored the many flaws inherent in California’s recall system. In November, voters will get a chance to remedy at least one of them, eliminating the chance a candidate could take office with just marginal support from voters.
